passages.happening:
“Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery to come upon you. Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes. Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire. You have hoarded treasure in the last days” (verses 1-3).

“Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts. You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the righteous, who did not resist you” (verses 4-6).
passages.hearers:
James now speaks like one of the old prophets. ‘Come now’ opens it, as in 4:13. But this time there is no call to repent, only a cry of judgment.

In the ancient world, wealth was often stored as fine clothes, gold and silver, and grain. Clothes could be eaten by moths; metals could tarnish. James speaks as if it has already happened: the riches have rotted. Their very rust will be a witness in court against their owners.

Then the heart of the charge. Large estates were worked by day labourers, hired by the day and paid each evening. A labourer who was not paid that night might not feed his family the next day. These landowners held the wages back. And the unpaid wages cry out, and the cries have reached ‘the Lord of Hosts’, the ancient title for God as commander of heaven's armies.

‘You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter’ is a grim picture: they have fed themselves full while judgment draws near. And verse 6 may speak of the poor ruined through the courts, or of real killings. James does not say.

Who are these rich men? James does not seem to expect them to read the letter. Like the prophets' words against foreign nations, these words are spoken over the oppressors for the sake of the oppressed. The poor believers hearing it would know that God had seen what was done to them.

James is not speaking against every person who has money, and his words are not a party's programme. He names particular wrongs: unpaid wages, luxury built on others' want, injustice in the courts. And the same wrongs are still done. Anyone who pays wages, or buys what others' labour makes, is inside the question.
passages.ot:
The law required prompt pay: “You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand” (Leviticus 19:13). And, “You are to pay his wages each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them. Otherwise he may cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin” (Deuteronomy 24:15).

The prophets spoke against those who cheated workers: “Woe to him who builds his palace by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms without justice, who makes his countrymen serve without pay, and fails to pay their wages” (Jeremiah 22:13). Malachi says God will be a witness “against those who defraud laborers of their wages” (Malachi 3:5).

And ‘the Lord of Hosts’ hears, as in Isaiah's woe on those who “add house to house and join field to field” (Isaiah 5:8): “I heard the LORD of Hosts declare” (Isaiah 5:9).
passages.asks: Ask whether anyone has been waiting on money you owe them. Ask how the people who make what you buy are paid. And if you have been cheated or crushed by the powerful, hear that God has heard the cries, and that the last word is his.

passages.t: Be patient until the Lord comes
passages.happening:
“Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord’s coming. See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil—how patient he is for the fall and spring rains. You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord’s coming is near” (verses 7-8).

“Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged. Look, the Judge is standing at the door! Brothers, as an example of patience in affliction, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. See how blessed we consider those who have persevered. You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy” (verses 9-11).

“Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath. Simply let your ‘Yes’ be yes, and your ‘No,’ no, so that you will not fall under judgment” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Now James turns to the poor believers who suffer under the rich. His word is not ‘take revenge’ but ‘be patient’. The word means ‘long-tempered’, able to bear hardship and people without hitting back or giving up.

The farmer is his first example. In the land, rain came in autumn, softening the ground for planting, and again in spring, filling out the grain before harvest. A farmer could do nothing to hurry it. He waited, and he trusted that the rain would come.

‘The Lord’s coming’ is the word parousia, used in the Greek world for a ruler's official visit to a city. The New Testament uses it for Christ's return. James says it is ‘near’, and that ‘the Judge is standing at the door’. He gives no date. The nearness shapes how believers live now: they need not take revenge, because the Judge is coming; and they must not grumble against one another, because that same Judge sees them too.

The second example is the prophets, who spoke for God and suffered for it. The third is Job. Job was not quietly patient; he cried out to God in pain and argument. But he did not let go of God. And he saw ‘the outcome from the Lord’: the God who is ‘full of compassion and mercy’.

Then oaths. In daily speech people swore constantly to make their word believable, often by heaven or earth to avoid using God's name. Jesus forbade this habit, and James repeats his teaching nearly word for word. Let your plain yes and no be enough.
passages.ot:
The farmer's rains are promised in the law: “then I will provide rain for your land in season, the autumn and spring rains, that you may gather your grain, new wine, and oil” (Deuteronomy 11:14).

The psalms teach the same patience: “Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him; do not fret when men prosper in their ways” (Psalm 37:7).

Job's story ends with God's kindness: “So the LORD blessed Job’s latter days more than his first” (Job 42:12). And James's last line echoes God's own name, spoken to Moses: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).

The law forbade false oaths: “You must not swear falsely by My name and so profane the name of your God” (Leviticus 19:12).
passages.hard:
Job got everything back in the end. Does James promise that patient people will always be rewarded in this life?

No. Job's story ends with God restoring him, and James points to that outcome as a sign of God's compassion. But the prophets James names as examples were often not rescued in this life. Many suffered to the end. James's hope is ‘the Lord's coming’, not a guarantee that everything will be put right before then.

Nor is ‘be patient’ a word to someone being abused or exploited that they must stay and bear it. James has just spoken fiercely against those who cheat and crush the poor. Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what you are waiting for, and whether you are waiting like a farmer, trusting, or like a judge, grumbling. Ask whom you have been complaining about. And ask whether your plain yes and no can be trusted, without any oath to prop them up.

passages.t: Pray: the suffering, the cheerful, the sick
passages.happening:
“Is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises” (verse 13).

“Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven. Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail” (verses 14-16).

“Elijah was a man just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops” (verses 17-18).
passages.hearers:
James ends with prayer. Whatever state a person is in, there is a way to bring it to God. Suffering? Pray. Cheerful? Sing. Sick? Call the church to pray.

‘The elders’ were the recognised leaders of the congregation, a pattern taken over from the synagogue. The sick person is not left alone. He calls, and the leaders come to him, pray over him, and anoint him with olive oil ‘in the name of the Lord’. In James's world olive oil was a medicine, poured on wounds and rubbed on the sick, and it was also used to mark a person as set apart for God. The word James uses for ‘anoint’ is the ordinary word for applying oil. Jesus' disciples had done the same: they “healed many of the sick, anointing them with oil” (Mark 6:13).

‘The prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up.’ The Greek words for ‘restore’ and ‘raise up’ can mean to heal and get someone up from a sickbed; they are also the words for ‘save’ and ‘raise’ from the dead.

‘If he has sinned’ is a careful phrase. James does not say the sickness came from sin. He says that if there is sin, it will be forgiven too. Then he widens it to everyone: confess your sins to each other and pray for each other. Healing in James includes the body and the whole person, and the whole church shares in it.

Last, Elijah. He was a great prophet, but James says he was ‘a man just like us’. He prayed, and the rain stopped; he prayed again, and it came. Prayer is not for spiritual giants only.
passages.ot:
Elijah's story is in 1 Kings. He told King Ahab, “there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word!” (1 Kings 17:1). After the drought, he went up to pray: “But Elijah climbed to the summit of Carmel, bent down on the ground, and put his face between his knees” (1 Kings 18:42). And “a heavy rain began to fall” (1 Kings 18:45).

The psalms show the sick crying to God: “O LORD my God, I cried to You for help, and You healed me” (Psalm 30:2). And they show the freedom of confession: “Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity” (Psalm 32:5). Proverbs adds, “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).
passages.hard:
Does James promise that anyone prayed for with faith will be healed? And if someone is not healed, was their faith too weak?

Christians read the promise in more than one way. All of them pray for the sick, as James tells the church to do. Many take it as a real promise of God's help, which often comes as healing in this life and comes fully in the resurrection, since the words for ‘restore’ and ‘raise up’ can carry both meanings. Others stress that healing depends on God's will, as Paul's own unhealed thorn shows (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). The Catholic and Orthodox churches see in these verses the ground of a sacrament, the anointing of the sick. Many Protestant churches see the oil as medicine, a sign, or both, and some anoint the sick with prayer as James describes. None of these readings sets prayer against medical care. Oil was itself a medicine.

James does not say that sickness comes from sin. ‘If he has sinned’ means that some may have, not that all have. When the disciples asked whose sin made a man blind, Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3).

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whether you bring every state of your life to God: suffering, joy, sickness, sin. If you are sick, ask whether you have let the church pray with you, as well as seeing a doctor. Ask whether there is someone you need to confess to. And ask whom you could pray for today, believing that prayer is not only for giants.

passages.t: Bring back the one who wanders
passages.happening: “My brothers, if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back, consider this: Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins” (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
The letter ends here, with no greetings and no farewell. Its last picture is a church going after one of its own.

‘Wander’ is the word for straying, as a sheep strays from the flock. The person James describes was ‘one of you’, a believer who has drifted from the truth, in what he believes or how he lives. And the call is not to the elders only. ‘Someone’ brings him back: any believer can.

The stakes are high: ‘death’ on one side, and on the other, ‘a multitude of sins’ covered. To ‘cover’ sins is the Bible's language for forgiveness, as in the psalm: “You forgave the iniquity of Your people; You covered all their sin” (Psalm 85:2). James does not say this is easy or always welcome. He says it is worth doing.

The last words of the letter gather up its whole concern. James has spoken of faith that acts, of mercy, of the tongue that can bless or curse. Now he points to the best use of a tongue and of faith that works: to go after someone who has wandered, and help them home.
passages.ot:
The prophets condemned shepherds who did not do this: “You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured, brought back the strays, or searched for the lost” (Ezekiel 34:4). And God promised to do it himself: “I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak” (Ezekiel 34:16).

The psalm sings of the God who brings his people back: “He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name” (Psalm 23:3).

And the line about covering sins echoes Proverbs: “Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions” (Proverbs 10:12).
passages.hard:
Does ‘bring him back’ mean that a church should chase, pressure or shame people who have left?

No. James is speaking of love, the kind that goes after a wandering friend the way a shepherd goes after a sheep. It is patient and humble, and it remembers that ‘We all stumble in many ways’ (3:2). It does not hound, threaten or shame.

Some people left a church because they were hurt there. Going after them begins with listening, and sometimes with confessing what the church did wrong. If you have been harmed by someone in a church, and were told to forgive and say nothing, what happened to you may have been wrong. Please talk with someone you trust outside that situation. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Think of someone who has drifted from the faith or from the church. Ask whether you have prayed for them, and whether you have gone to them with love rather than pressure. Ask whether you need to listen before you speak. And ask whether you have ever been brought back yourself, and by whom.
